tldr: Scideator is the first human-LLM compound system for scientific ideation that maintains a shared faceted representation (purposes, mechanisms, evaluations) across retrieval, generation, and novelty evaluation modules, enabling iterative idea creation and assessment through structured facet-level interactions.
contributions: Scideator, the first human-LLM compound system for scientific ideation with a single faceted representation across retrieval, generation, novelty evaluation, and suggestion, where users can select, modify, or build on outputs at each stage.

A within-subjects user study (N=22) showing Scideator provides significantly more creativity support than a baseline using the same LLM without faceted interaction, with participants discovering new concepts through the system's facets and preferring facet-level steering over prompting.

Evaluation of the novelty checker demonstrating that facet-based re-ranking improves paper selection for novelty assessment over general-relevance re-ranking and embedding-only retrieval, and facet-grounded classification independently outperforms baseline novelty checkers on the same retrieved papers.
methods: Scideator comprises three LLM-powered modules operating in an iterative loop. Module 1 (Analogous Paper Facet Finder) extracts purpose, mechanism, and evaluation facets from input papers, generates analogous purpose-mechanism pairs at three distance levels (near, far, very far), retrieves corresponding papers from Semantic Scholar, and extracts facets from all retrieved papers. Module 2 (Faceted Idea Generator) recombines selected facets through analogy, generating candidate analogies between papers from different distance groups and converting the strongest analogies into recombinant ideas. Module 3 (Idea Novelty Checker) uses a retrieve-then-rerank pipeline: it gathers candidate papers via keyword search and snippet-text search, re-ranks them with SPECTER embeddings followed by facet-based LLM re-ranking with RankGPT, classifies ideas as novel or not novel using expert-labeled in-context examples, and suggests facet swaps for non-novel ideas. A within-subjects user study with 22 computer science researchers compared Scideator against a baseline using the same backbone LLM without faceted modules.
results: Participants experienced significantly more creativity support with Scideator, particularly in exploring different ideas. When using Scideator, participants cited the tool's facets or ideas as the source of new concepts, whereas with the baseline they most often cited input papers. Participants tended to lower their idea novelty assessments when Scideator classified an idea as 'not novel,' and they could verify classifications using provided related papers and explanations. Ablation studies showed that facet-based re-ranking ranks relevant prior work higher than general-relevance re-ranking or embedding-only retrieval. Keeping retrieval constant, facet-grounded classification outperformed classifiers that reason over ideas and papers as wholes. Expert annotation inter-annotator agreement was moderate (Cohen's κ = 0.64 initially, improving to κ = 0.68 after revision), with 67 consensus-labeled examples collected.
limitations: Facets are constrained to short phrases (no more than 7 words), which may not always be immediately clear, especially for facets from distant domains. The novelty classification relies on retrieved papers rather than annotators' broader background knowledge, and expert annotation agreement was only moderate (Cohen's κ = 0.68). The user study was limited to 22 computer science researchers, restricting generalizability.
